name: Proposal Copy Count
queries: In the CAJPA sample investment management RFP (Appendix Z, 'Sample Investment Management Request for Proposal'), how many copies of the proposal must be sent?
description: The evidence states in the proposal delivery section that six copies of the proposal must be received. It also notes that electronic submission is acceptable as an alternative if received by the stated deadline.
content: In the sample investment management RFP, the required number of hard copies is six (6). The relevant language appears in Part 6, Section 6.2 (“RFP Due Date & Delivery”), which says: “Six (6) copies of the proposal must be received by IMRF…” The evidence also adds that: - the six copies must be received by the specified deadline, - they must be addressed and delivered to IMRF at the listed Oak Brook, Illinois address, and - electronic submission is also acceptable if sent by email before the same deadline. So, the answer to how many copies must be sent is: six copies.

name: Reference Requirement
queries: In the Boston Retirement System's investment consulting services proposal questionnaire (Attachment 3), how many current public fund client references must be listed, and what minimum asset size must those clients have?
description: Attachment 3 of the Boston Retirement System investment consulting services proposal questionnaire specifies the required public fund client references in section D.2. It requires a list of up to 10 current public fund clients, and those clients must each have assets greater than $1 billion.
content:
In Attachment 3, section D.2 states: “Provide a list of up to 10 current public fund clients with assets greater than $1 billion for whom work similar to that requested in this RFP has been performed by your firm.”

So, the questionnaire requires:
- Number of current public fund client references to be listed: up to 10
- Minimum asset size for those clients: greater than $1 billion

name: FPIF private markets split.
queries: In the Illinois Firefighters' Pension Investment Fund (FPIF) February 2023 RFP for private markets investment consulting and discretionary OCIO advisory services, what long-term target allocation to private markets is FPIF building, and how is it split across asset classes?
description: The evidence directly states FPIF’s long-term target allocation to private markets and its asset-class breakdown in the February 2023 RFP. It also notes how the real estate and infrastructure targets are further divided between core open-ended vehicles and non-core commitments.
content:
In FPIF’s February 2023 RFP, the fund says it is constructing a long-term target allocation of 31% to private market asset classes.

That 31% target is split as follows:
- 10% to private equity
- 7% to private debt
- 10% to real estate
- 4% to infrastructure

The RFP also specifies an additional detail for real estate and infrastructure:
- Of the 10% real estate target and 4% infrastructure target, 50% is intended for core open-ended vehicles
- The remaining 50% is intended for non-core commitments

So, in short, FPIF’s long-term private markets buildout is 31% total, allocated across private equity, private debt, real estate, and infrastructure in a 10% / 7% / 10% / 4% split.

name: $10B PE experience minimum.
queries: In the Teachers' Retirement System of the State of Illinois (TRS) FY25 RFP for private equity investment consultant services, what minimum private equity client experience must a firm certify?
description: The evidence states that the TRS FY25 private equity investment consultant RFP requires a firm to certify a minimum level of private equity consulting experience. Specifically, the firm and/or its principals must have served clients whose private equity portfolio assets total at least $10 billion in aggregate.
content:
The minimum private equity client experience a firm must certify is that the firm and/or its principals have experience providing private equity consulting services to clients with at least $10 billion in aggregate private equity portfolio assets.

This requirement appears in Appendix B, Statement of Minimum Qualifications, which specifies that the proposer must certify this threshold as part of the minimum qualifications. In other words, the relevant experience standard is not based simply on number of clients, but on the combined size of the private equity portfolios of the clients served.

name: 2010 real assets totals
queries: A real assets investment consulting solicitation states that the funds' strategic asset allocation targets were adopted by the Board in 2003. As of September 30, 2010, how much did the Board have in its separate account private real estate program, its separate account private infrastructure program, and public real estate securities, and how large were its unfunded commitments?
description: The solicitation states the Board’s real assets holdings as of September 30, 2010, including amounts in private real estate, private infrastructure, public real estate securities, and unfunded commitments. These figures directly answer the question.
content:
As of September 30, 2010, the Board had approximately:

- $164 million invested in a separate account private real estate investment program
- $59 million invested in a separate account private infrastructure investment program
- $25 million invested in public real estate securities

In addition, the Board had approximately $88 million in unfunded commitments to real estate and infrastructure funds.

name: Track record and clients.
queries: An investment manager RFP template for an emerging markets equity strategy (issued February 14, 2022, responses due March 31, 2022) lists required minimum qualifications and 'preferred criteria'. What live track record does it require, and what public pension client base does it prefer?
description: The February 14, 2022 SURS emerging markets equity RFP template requires a live track record of at least 5 years for the proposed strategy. Its preferred public pension client base is either at least two existing U.S. public pension fund clients with over $1 billion in total plan assets, or at least one existing public plan client with over $10 billion in total plan assets.
content:
In the “Required Minimum Qualifications,” the template states that the proposing firm must have an established “live” track record of at least 5 years managing the proposed emerging markets equity strategy as of 12/31/20__, with an exemption noted for qualified Women-, Minority-, or Disabled-Owned Businesses, which may still be considered at SURS’ discretion.

In the “Preferred Criteria,” the template states that the firm is preferred to have either:
1. at least two existing U.S. public pension fund clients with over $1 billion in total plan assets, or
2. at least one existing public plan client with over $10 billion in total plan assets.

So, the required live track record is 5 years, and the preferred public pension client base is two $1B+ U.S. public pension clients or one $10B+ public plan client.

name: Approximate portfolio NAVs
queries: An alternative investment consulting RFP describes a private equity portfolio of 225 holdings across 105 general partners. What are the approximate net asset values of the system's absolute return, private credit, private equity and real assets portfolios?
description: The relevant evidence indicates approximate net asset values for the alternative portfolios referenced in the RFP with the private equity portfolio described as having 225 holdings across 105 general partners. The figures are given as approximate NAVs for absolute return, private credit, private equity, and real assets.
content:
The approximate net asset values are:

- Absolute return: approximately $2.6 billion
- Private credit: approximately $1.8 billion
- Private equity: approximately $4.5 billion
- Real assets: approximately $3.1 billion

The private equity figure corresponds to the portfolio described in the RFP as having about 225 holdings across 105 general partners.

name: IMRF selection factors.
queries: In the Illinois Municipal Retirement Fund (IMRF) sample RFP for investment consulting, real estate consulting and performance measurement services, on what factors are respondents evaluated and ranked during the selection process?
description: In the IMRF sample RFP for investment consulting, real estate consulting, and performance measurement services, respondents are evaluated and ranked on three stated factors during the selection process. The RFP specifies organization, consulting skill, and fees as the basis for ranking.
content:
According to Part 8.1, “Selection Process,” of the IMRF sample RFP for investment consulting, real estate consulting and performance measurement services, all respondents are evaluated and ranked based upon the following factors:

1. Organization  
   - Stability  
   - Ownership  
   - Documented experience of key professionals  

2. Consulting Skill  
   - Investment philosophy  
   - Investment manager information collection and monitoring systems  
   - Risk management tools  
   - Performance measurement systems  
   - Breadth of consulting expertise and experience  

3. Fees  
   - Consulting fees for the services requested  
   - Associated costs  

The RFP also notes that IMRF staff objectively reviews proposals based solely on the criteria presented in the RFP, may interview respondents and conduct site visits or other due diligence, and then presents a report to the Investment Committee. In addition, staff must identify minority- and women-owned firms and firms owned by persons with a disability in the report, and must specify why such firms are not advanced as finalists if that occurs.

name: IMRF ranking factors.
queries: In the Illinois Municipal Retirement Fund (IMRF) sample RFP for domestic equity small cap growth investment management, on what factors are respondents evaluated and ranked during the selection process?
description: In the IMRF sample RFP for domestic equity small cap growth investment management, respondents are evaluated and ranked on four primary factors during the selection process. These factors are people, process, performance, and pricing.
content:
During the selection process, IMRF states that all respondents to the RFP are evaluated and ranked on four primary factors:

1. People — stability of the organization, ownership structure, and documented experience of key professionals.
2. Process — a clearly defined, reasonable, and repeatable investment strategy.
3. Performance — documented ability to meet investment performance benchmarks.
4. Pricing — fee schedule and associated costs.

The RFP also explains that IMRF staff and its consultant objectively review proposals based solely on the criteria presented in the RFP. They may also interview respondents, conduct site visits, and perform other due diligence before making recommendations to the Investment Committee and ultimately the Board.

name: PRIM AUM minimum
queries: In the Massachusetts PRIM Board's October 2023 RFP for Multi-Asset Credit investment management services, what minimum total firm assets under management must a respondent have?
description: The relevant evidence states that, in the Massachusetts PRIM Board’s October 2023 RFP for Multi-Asset Credit investment management services, a respondent must meet a minimum firm-size threshold. Specifically, the respondent must have at least $10 billion in total firm assets under management, measured as of September 30, 2023.
content:
In the Massachusetts PRIM Board’s October 2023 RFP for Multi-Asset Credit investment management services, a respondent must have a minimum of $10 billion in total firm assets under management.

The evidence also notes that this appears in Section VI, “Minimum Qualifications,” item 4, and that the qualification can alternatively be satisfied by having at least $2 billion in multi-asset credit strategy assets under management. The measurement date for this requirement is September 30, 2023.

Because the question asks specifically for the minimum total firm assets under management, the answer is: $10 billion.

name: BCERS 7-Year Requirement
queries: In the Baltimore City Employees' Retirement Systems (BCERS) RFP for an alternatives consultant, how many years must the proposing firm have been in business?
description: The BCERS alternatives consultant RFP states the proposing firm must meet a minimum business-history requirement. Specifically, the firm must have been in business for at least seven years.
content:
In Section I.E, “Minimum Qualifications,” the BCERS RFP says: “The firm must have been in business for at least seven (7) or more years providing general consulting services plus private equity consulting services or alternatives consulting services only.”

So, the proposing firm must have been in business for at least 7 years.

Relevant context:
- This is a minimum qualification.
- Failure to satisfy the minimum qualifications may result in immediate rejection of the proposal.
- All minimum qualifications had to be met as of November 8, 2024, at 3:00 p.m. EDT.

name: SBCERS five-year rule.
queries: In the Santa Barbara County Employees' Retirement System (SBCERS) 2020 RFP for a discretionary private equity consultant, how many years must the proposing firm have been in business?
description: The SBCERS 2020 RFP explicitly states the minimum business-history requirement for proposing firms. Under “Minimum Qualifications for Proposal,” the firm must have been in business at least five years.
content:
In the Santa Barbara County Employees’ Retirement System (SBCERS) 2020 Request for Proposals for Discretionary Private Equity Consultant Services, the proposing firm must have been in business for at least five (5) years.

This requirement appears in Section I.F, “Minimum Qualifications for Proposal,” item 1, which states: “The firm must have been in business at least five (5) years providing services similar to those described in the Scope of Services section.”

So the answer is: at least 5 years.

name: PSPRS RFP scoring weights.
queries: What evaluation criteria and weights does the Arizona Public Safety Personnel Retirement System (PSPRS) use in its RFP for non-discretionary investment consultant services?
description: The Arizona PSPRS RFP for non-discretionary investment consultant services evaluates proposals using four weighted criteria. The weights are explicitly stated in the RFP and apply to written submissions and, if held, finalist interviews.
content:
Arizona PSPRS uses the following evaluation criteria and weights in its RFP for non-discretionary investment consultant services:

1. 25% — Relevant knowledge and experience  
   - Relevant knowledge and experience in similar consulting engagements  
   - Current organizational capacity to provide experienced staff  
   - Ability to perform the services described in the Scope of Services

2. 30% — Quality and extent of firm capabilities  
   This is the most heavily weighted category. It covers the firm’s capabilities in:
   - Strategic advice  
   - New investment identification and evaluation  
   - Operational due diligence  
   - Investment due diligence  
   - Manager performance reporting and monitoring  
   - Back office support

3. 25% — Demonstrated ability to meet service requirements  
   This includes:
   - Ability to communicate with the CIO and investment team  
   - Ability to communicate with Trustees and the Board’s consultant  
   - Responsiveness on ongoing and special issues  
   - Operational plan for fulfilling duties  
   - Quality of professional staff assigned to the contract

4. 20% — Overall cost  
   - Overall cost of the firm’s proposed services

Additional note from the RFP:
- Proposals are evaluated based on written submissions and/or finalist interviews.
- Interviews are not guaranteed, so firms are instructed to include all relevant information in their written proposals.

name: BCERS quarterly minimums.
queries: Under the Baltimore City Employees' Retirement Systems (BCERS) alternatives consultant RFP, what must the consultant's quarterly performance report include at a minimum?
description: Under the BCERS Alternatives Consultant RFP, the quarterly performance report has a defined minimum content list in the reporting requirements section. It must cover market context, portfolio allocation, fund-level details, and aggregated portfolio metrics.
content:
Under Section I.D.(5)(a) of the BCERS Alternatives Consultant RFP, the consultant’s quarterly performance report must include, at a minimum:

1. Market overview and outlook.
2. Allocation breakdown by geography, strategy, and industry.
3. An update on each fund.
4. A listing of each fund by strategy.
5. The date of commitment to each fund.
6. The commitment amount to each fund.
7. Drawdown amounts by fund.
8. Outstanding commitment by fund.
9. Distribution amounts by fund.
10. Fund net asset values.
11. IRR and multiples of each fund.
12. Items 6 through 11 aggregated for:
   - the core private equity portfolio,
   - the specialized portfolio, and
   - the total portfolio (core and specialized).

The RFP also separately requires the consultant to reconcile monthly and quarterly reports with the records of the BCERS custodian bank and provide any other reporting required by BCERS’ Accounting Division.

name: Required IMRF Meetings
queries: Which meetings must the investment consultant attend under the IMRF sample RFP for investment consulting, real estate consulting and performance measurement services, and how many days of meetings per year does IMRF estimate?
description: The IMRF sample RFP requires the investment consultant to attend a defined set of meetings with Board members and/or staff. The RFP also gives IMRF’s estimate of the total annual meeting time required.
content:
Under the IMRF sample RFP for investment consulting, real estate consulting, and performance measurement services, the investment consultant must attend the following meetings with IMRF Board members and/or staff, on-site and off-site:

1. Monthly IMRF Board meetings  
2. Investment Committee meetings  
3. Annual IMRF Roundtable  
4. Regional meetings with investment managers  
5. Related investment meetings and discussions  
6. Formal interviews with existing and potential investment managers  
7. Ad hoc due diligence meetings with investment managers and Staff  

IMRF states in the RFP that, to complete these activities, it estimates there will be sixty days of meetings annually with the Board of Trustees and/or members of the staff.

The RFP also adds that there will be frequent telephone discussions with Staff relating to all investment issues covered by the assignment.

name: PRIM evaluation criteria.
queries: What selection criteria will the Evaluation Committee use to assess respondents to the Massachusetts PRIM Active Global Core Equity Investment Management Services RFP (September 2026)?
description: The evidence directly identifies the Evaluation Committee’s criteria for the Massachusetts PRIM Active Global Core Equity Investment Management Services RFP (September 2026). It also notes that proposals must first satisfy submission requirements and minimum qualifications before being evaluated on those criteria. The criteria are not necessarily ranked by importance or weighted equally.
content:
For the Massachusetts PRIM Active Global Core Equity Investment Management Services RFP (September 2026), the Evaluation Committee will assess respondents using these selection criteria:

1. Organizational stability, ownership structure, and firm experience.
2. Experience, stability, depth, and continuity of the team proposed for the PRIM account.
3. Clarity, consistency, and repeatability of the investment philosophy and process, including alignment with the mandate described in the RFP.
4. Historical track record and performance relative to the MSCI ACWI IMI across market cycles.
5. Breadth and depth of research capabilities.
6. Portfolio construction and risk management, including the firm’s approach to tracking error, active risk, and exposures relative to the MSCI ACWI IMI.
7. Capacity to manage the mandate in a separately managed account without degrading the strategy, including current and remaining product capacity.
8. Operational infrastructure.
9. Quality and relevance of client references.
10. Competitiveness of proposed fees.

Additional evaluation note:
- Before applying these criteria, PRIM will first determine whether each response was submitted in accordance with the RFP requirements and meets the Minimum Qualifications.
- Responses that fail the Minimum Qualifications will be rejected.
- PRIM states that the criteria are not necessarily listed in order of importance and are not necessarily weighted equally.

  - June 30, 2024
  - June 30, 2026

- Biennial OPEB roll-forward updates as of:

name: Audit firm and term limit.
queries: In the Indiana Public Retirement System (INPRS) RFP 24-05 for audit services, which firm has provided INPRS's external audit services and since when, and what limit does INPRS's procurement policy place on contract length?
description: The RFP states that RSM has served as INPRS’s external auditor since 2014. It also says INPRS procurement policy limits contract length to 10 years and requires new bids at least every 10 years. The RFP’s contract section is consistent with that policy, capping the total contract period at 10 years.
content: In INPRS RFP 24-05 for audit services, the document says that RSM has provided INPRS’s external audit services since 2014. The RFP also explains that INPRS’s procurement policy, as stated in the INPRS Board Governance Manual, limits contract length to 10 years and requires solicitation of new bids no less frequently than every 10 years. name: Model Plan minimums.
queries: A county 457(b) deferred compensation plan RFP subject to the rules of the New York State Deferred Compensation Board states a minimum deferral amount required by the Model Plan. What is that minimum, and within how many business days must participant deferrals be invested?
description: The New York State Deferred Compensation Board Model Plan provisions quoted in the county 457(b) RFP directly answer both parts of the question. They state the minimum annual deferral and the deadline for investing participant deferrals after receipt.
content:
According to the county 457(b) deferred compensation plan RFP that operates under the New York State Deferred Compensation Board Rules and the State Model Plan:

- **Minimum deferral amount required by the Model Plan:** **$260 for any plan year**
  - This appears in **Specifications of the Model Plan, Section 3.2(a)**, which states that the Model Plan requires a minimum deferral amount of **$260** for any plan year.

- **Deadline for investing participant deferrals:** **no later than 2 business days following receipt**
  - This appears in **Specifications of the Model Plan, Section 4.1**, which states that amounts deferred by participants must be invested according to the participant’s investment directions **no later than two (2) business days following receipt thereof**.

So, the answer is: **$260 minimum per plan year, and deferrals must be invested within 2 business days after receipt.**

name: TMRS custody scoring
queries: What evaluation criteria and percentage weights does the Texas Municipal Retirement System (TMRS) global custody RFP use to evaluate respondents?
description: The evidence directly provides the TMRS global custody RFP evaluation framework, including four weighted categories and their percentage allocations. It also notes that TMRS staff and RVK, Inc. evaluate respondents using proposals, follow-up information, and interviews or presentations if requested.
content:
TMRS’s global custody RFP evaluates respondents using the following criteria and percentage weights:

1. Scope affirmation, servicing approach, and institutional credentials — 25%
   This category covers:
   - Ability to provide the required scope of services
   - Institutional experience, particularly with public fund portfolios
   - Depth of custody products and service deliverables
   - Availability and quality of key professionals and the servicing team
   - Financial condition, credit ratings, and commitment to the custody business
   - Potential or actual material conflicts of interest
   - Ability to mitigate transition challenges and risks

2. Core and value-added services and technology platforms — 40%
   This is the highest-weighted category and includes:
   - Systems and technology infrastructure
   - Custody and core accounting platform
   - Performance measurement and analytical capabilities
   - Alternative investment services and related analytical platform

3. Quality of response and additional evidence of capability — 10%
   This includes:
   - Overall quality of the written proposal
   - Quality of any oral presentation
   - Samples and follow-up evidence demonstrating capability with similar institutional clients

4. Competitiveness and reasonableness of economics — 25%
   This includes:
   - Proposed fees evaluated in relation to service quality
   - TMRS’s statement that it may or may not select the lowest-cost respondent
   - Consideration of transition cost and transition risk, including for an incumbent provider

Additional relevant evaluation process details:
- TMRS staff and RVK, Inc. evaluate respondents.
- Evaluation may be based on:
  - Written proposals
  - Any additional written information requested
  - Oral interviews or presentations, if any
- TMRS may identify one or more finalists after initial review.
- Finalists may be asked to provide:
  - On-site or virtual presentations
  - References
  - Responses to follow-up due diligence questions
  - A best-and-final fee proposal

name: Temple City RFP minimums.
queries: What minimum qualifications must a proposing firm certify in the City of Temple City's 2020 RFP for 457 plan administration and recordkeeping services?
description: The evidence directly answers the question in Section III, “Minimum Qualifications,” of the City of Temple City’s 2020 RFP. It lists the specific certifications each proposing firm had to meet or agree to for 457 plan administration and recordkeeping services.
content:
In the City of Temple City’s 2020 RFP for 457 plan administration and recordkeeping services, each proposing firm was required to certify that it met or agreed to the following minimum qualifications:

1. The firm must have at least five (5) years of experience administering governmental Section 457 deferred compensation plans, and it must currently provide sole-provider administration to at least five (5) Section 457 deferred compensation retirement plans with assets under $25 million.

2. Any contract must provide that there will be no front-end charges or back-end charges. There also may be no restrictions or penalties on plan-initiated or participant-initiated transfers or withdrawals, including contract termination, except for:
   - capital preservation equity wash and/or put provisions related to stable value or fixed/general account products, and/or
   - mutual-fund-specific short-term trading fees.

3. The firm must accurately and fully disclose all fund expenses and all revenue-sharing arrangements associated with every fund offered in the plan. This disclosure requirement also applies to fixed or general account products, and firms offering those products must provide an accurate assessment of product expenses and revenue remitted to the firm.

4. The firm must accurately and fully disclose all expenses and revenue associated with any service made available under the plan, including services such as:
   - platform fees,
   - managed accounts,
   - investment advice,
   - financial planning, and
   - self-directed brokerage accounts.

5. The firm must agree by contract not to sell or promote products not directly affiliated with the plan unless the City gives specific written authorization.

6. Upon award of the contract, the selected firm must be duly qualified to do business in the State of California and in the City of Temple City.

7. The organization must be able to offer a self-directed brokerage option.

8. The firm must be able to transition and continue administration of existing plan loans, if needed.

9. The firm must be willing to have representatives attend City meetings in person when requested, no more than once per year.

10. The firm must know and comply with all applicable County, State of California, and federal regulations governing governmental retirement plans and investment options. 11. The terms presented throughout the RFP process, including the firm’s response and any later enhancements, must remain in place through negotiations and become part of the final contract unless the City specifically waives them in writing.

name: OCERS PAS oversight scope.
queries: What project oversight services does OCERS require from the consultant in its 2023 RFP for Pension Administration Project Oversight and Consultation Services?
description: OCERS’ 2023 RFP requires the consultant to provide on-site project oversight and project management support for selecting and implementing a new Pension Administration System (PAS). The consultant is expected to manage planning, procurement support, implementation oversight, reporting, risk/issues/change control, quality assurance, stakeholder coordination, and post-implementation support to help ensure the project is delivered on time, within budget, and according to requirements.
content:
In its September 2023 RFP for Pension Administration Project Oversight and Consultation Services, OCERS requires the consultant to serve as an implementation partner providing full-time, on-site oversight project management, staff support, and quality assurance for the selection and implementation of a new Pension Administration System (PAS).

Key required project oversight services include:

1. Overall project oversight and management
- Provide project management and quality oversight for the selection and implementation of the new PAS.
- Help OCERS manage and oversee the full implementation process through active participation, review, facilitation, and guidance.
- Ensure the new system meets project requirements, stays on schedule, and remains within budget.
- Coordinate with OCERS’ Enterprise Project Management Office (EPMO).

2. Planning and early project definition
- Coordinate planning tasks tied to requirements definition, solutions design, and the IT strategic roadmap.
- Perform a needs and requirements assessment.
- Facilitate gathering departmental wants and needs for the new PAS.
- Incorporate OCERS strategic initiatives, including future-oriented capabilities such as Robotic Process Automation (RPA), Machine Learning (ML), Artificial Intelligence, and Intelligent Automation.
- Create a staffing plan.
- Create an IT Strategic Roadmap plan.
- Develop the PAS implementation project plan and overall implementation approach.
- Identify project milestones and resource needs throughout the project.

3. RFP development and procurement support
- Write the RFP(s) for required software applications and/or services.
- Prepare a concise and comprehensive RFP for the new PAS.
- Coordinate the procurement process with OCERS staff.
- Facilitate and advise on vendor selection activities, including:
  - software demonstrations,
  - vendor interviews,
  - evaluation of BAFO submissions,
  - final vendor selection.

4. Vendor and contract oversight
- Coordinate and manage vendors.
- Ensure vendors meet the requirements matrix.
- Ensure PAS vendor(s) satisfy all RFP requirements and have an approach/strategy for each required item.
- Review PAS vendor contracts.
- Perform services cooperatively with OCERS staff, including Procurement, Legal, IT, and Member Services.

5. Implementation oversight
- Oversee and coordinate design, development, testing, training, and implementation activities for the new PAS.
- Work with OCERS and PAS vendor(s) on the overall conversion strategy, including:
  - data cleansing,
  - data migration,
  - data conversion.
- Establish procedures for requirements gathering with OCERS and the PAS vendor.

6. Deliverables management and documentation review
- Provide project management reports and metrics for accurate status and due-date reporting.
- Develop, review, and comment on project deliverables and documentation, including:
  - Statements of Work and task descriptions,
  - data conversion plans and reconciliation procedures,
  - system test plans, scripts, and test cases,
  - user acceptance plans and acceptance criteria,
  - project schedules,
  - cutover plans, timelines, and processes.

7. Governance, approvals, and methodology
- Establish a sign-off process and ensure adequate sign-off procedures are followed throughout the system development life cycle.
- Ensure a rigorous project methodology, plan, and schedule are proposed and followed.
- Ensure any schedule changes are properly reflected in the project plan.

8. Communications, issues, risk, and change control
- Ensure project issues and status are properly communicated.
- Manage project issues and escalate them appropriately and promptly when needed.
- Identify and address project risks for proper management.
- Ensure change control procedures are followed.

9. Quality assurance and testing
- Provide quality assurance as part of the oversight role.
- Develop testing procedures to ensure a high level of quality.

10. Stakeholder coordination and reporting
- Prepare a monthly oversight status report.
- Present the monthly status report to both the Steering Committee and the OCERS Board of Retirement.
- Provide project updates to external stakeholders as requested by the Steering Committee.
- Facilitate meetings and implementation oversight activities with external stakeholders such as employers and third-party vendors.
- Agree on a common glossary of terms for use across project teams.

11. Organizational change and training
- Work with OCERS to provide leadership in Organizational Change Management (OCM).
- Support staff training on the PAS throughout the project.

12. Post-implementation support
- Provide post-implementation support, with the final scope and duration to be mutually agreed upon.

13. Other project management support
- Address other project management issues that could hinder successful completion of the project.

Additional context from the RFP
- The engagement is envisioned as full-time.
- The expected project start date is approximately February 2024.
- The PAS implementation is estimated to take about 3 years.
- The consultant’s services must be provided on-site.

name: GASB 68 RFP coverage.
queries: Which audit-services RFP documents in the corpus cover audits of GASB Statement No. 68 schedules, and what does each say about that work?
description: In the provided evidence, the audit-services RFP that clearly covers audits of GASB Statement No. 68 schedules is the Indiana Public Retirement System (INPRS) RFP No. 24-05. It treats GASB 68 schedule work as a defined scope item, specifies the plans and schedules to be audited, and adds a required independent review of actuarial assumptions, methods, and procedures.
content:
- **Document identified:**  
  **Indiana Public Retirement System (INPRS) Request for Proposals for Audit Services, RFP Number 24-05**.

- **Where GASB 68 appears:**  
  The RFP mentions GASB 68 in two key places:
  1. **Section 2.4 – Fee Proposal**: respondents must provide proposed fees for each service category, specifically including **“GASB Statement No. 68 Schedules.”**
  2. **Section 3.2 – Services Required – GASB Statement No. 68 Schedules**: this section defines the required work.

- **What the RFP says about the GASB 68 work:**  
  Under **Section 3.2**, the selected auditor must:

  1. **Perform an annual audit and express an opinion** on the following schedules:
     - the **Schedule of Employer Allocation**, and
     - the related **Schedule of Pension Amounts by Employer**
     
     for these INPRS plans:
     - **Public Employee Retirement Fund (PERF)**
     - **Teachers’ Retirement Fund Pre 1996 Account (TRF Pre 1996)**
     - **Teachers’ Retirement Fund Post 1996 Account (TRF 1996)**
     - **the 1977 Fund**

  2. Also audit the related schedules for **TRF Pre-1996**, specifically:
     - the **Schedule of Non-Employer Allocation**
     - the related **Schedule of Employer Pension Amounts**
     - the **Schedule of Employer Allocation of Special Funding Situation Amounts**

  3. **Perform an independent review of actuarial work**, including:
     - actuarial assumptions,
     - methods, and
     - procedures  
     
     used by INPRS’s actuary to calculate:
     - the **total pension liability**, and
     - **employer contributions** for the plan.

     The RFP says this review must be done **in accordance with generally accepted actuarial principles and practices as set forth in Actuarial Standard of Practice No. 4**.

  4. **Address completed reports to the INPRS Board of Trustees.**

  5. **Complete the GASB 68 audits and issue the audit reports by January 31 of each year**, for INPRS’s **June 30 fiscal year end**.

- **Related proposal requirement tied to this work:**  
  In **Section 2.4**, firms must separately provide **details, estimated hours, and hourly rates** for the GASB 68 schedule work as part of the fee proposal.

- **Other documents in the provided evidence:**  
  The SDCERS document shown is a **general investment consultant RFP**, not an audit-services RFP, and it does **not** provide relevant GASB 68 audit-schedule scope. So, based on the evidence provided here, **INPRS RFP 24-05 is the relevant audit-services RFP document covering GASB Statement No. 68 schedule audits**.

name: 457 RFP term summary.
queries: What contract terms (initial length and any renewal or extension options) do the deferred compensation / 457 plan recordkeeping RFPs in the corpus propose?
description: In the provided deferred compensation / 457 plan recordkeeping RFPs, one RFP leaves the contract term to be negotiated, while another specifies a term of up to five years. The evidence does not support any broader corpus-wide renewal pattern beyond those stated terms.
content:
- **City of Temple City, California – 457 Deferred Compensation Plan RFP (2020):**
  - The RFP does **not set a fixed initial contract length**.
  - Instead, it states: **“The contract term will be negotiated at the conclusion of this RFP process.”**
  - It also says proposing firms may provide pricing for **different term structures**.
  - In the fee section, the City notes it is interested in **longer-term pricing**, but that purchasing requirements **may limit the maximum term to five years**.
  - The pricing tables specifically ask for proposals for:
    - **5-year**
    - **7-year**
    - **10-year**
  - For the **7-year and 10-year** options, the RFP explains these assume the City would **extend the contract at the appropriate time**, meaning those are not guaranteed base terms but rather **possible extended-term pricing scenarios**.
  - So, for Temple City:
    - **Initial length:** not specified; to be negotiated
    - **Renewal/extension options:** not formally awarded in the RFP text, but vendors were asked to quote **5-, 7-, and 10-year structures**, with 7- and 10-year terms dependent on later extension

- **Monroe County Deferred Compensation Plan RFP (2023):**
  - The RFP says the County expects to enter into a written contractual arrangement **“of up to five (5) years in duration.”**
  - This functions as the proposed contract term ceiling.
  - The contract is also stated to be **subject to periodic review by the Committee**.
  - The Committee may **cancel the contract at the end of any contract year** by giving **30 days’ advance written notice**.
  - The RFP does **not describe separate renewal option periods** beyond the stated **up to five years**.
  - So, for Monroe County:
    - **Initial length:** up to **5 years**
    - **Renewal/extension options:** none specifically stated beyond that overall term
    - **Related provision:** cancellable at the end of any contract year with 30 days’ notice

- **Irrelevant evidence excluded:**
  - The City of Austin Employees’ Retirement System RFP is for **actuarial services for a defined benefit plan**, not a deferred compensation / 457 recordkeeping RFP, so it is not relevant to the user’s question.

## Bottom line
Across the relevant evidence provided:
- One 457 recordkeeping RFP (**Temple City**) leaves the contract length **open for negotiation**, while soliciting pricing for **5-, 7-, and 10-year structures**, with longer periods dependent on extension.
- Another (**Monroe County**) proposes a contract of **up to five years**, with **no separate renewal schedule stated**.

name: Section 3.3 questions
queries: What questions does the INREV DDQ 2022 for Funds of Funds and Multi Manager ask under section 3.3 'IT, Cyber and Physical Security'?
description: The evidence directly includes the INREV DDQ 2022 for Funds of Funds / Multi Manager and lists all questions under section 3.3 “IT, Cyber and Physical Security.” Below is a faithful synthesis of those questions only, excluding irrelevant material.
content:
Under section 3.3 “IT, Cyber and Physical Security,” the INREV DDQ 2022 for Funds of Funds and Multi Manager asks the following questions:

1. 3.3.1 — Describe the position, responsibilities, and members of the IT function in the organisation. Provide an overview of outsourced IT activities and how outsourced vendors are monitored/controlled.

2. 3.3.2 — Are you compliant with International Organization for Standardization (ISO) 27001 or any other cyber security or information security certifications?

3. 3.3.3 — Is IT and physical security a standing item on your board (or equivalent) agenda?

4. 3.3.4 — Have you developed a formal, documented Cyber Incident Response Plan that describes workflow in the event of a cyber incident?

5. 3.3.5 — Have you experienced any material internal or external information/cyber security incident in the past three years?

6. 3.3.6 — Are all servers, workstations and remote devices connecting to corporate networks required to have approved antivirus software installed?

7. 3.3.7 — How frequently do you carry out IT security training for staff?

8. 3.3.8 — Do you carry out phishing or similar social engineering tests on your staff?

9. 3.3.9 — How frequently are full (physical and system) vulnerability assessments carried out?

10. 3.3.10 — How frequently are internal and external penetration tests carried out?

11. 3.3.11 — Are there any critical or high-risk points from any penetration tests or vulnerability assessments that are currently outstanding and have been so for over six months?

12. 3.3.12 — Have you engaged with an external cyber security specialist as a first point of contact in the event of an incident?

13. 3.3.13 — How is physical access to the server/communication room controlled?

14. 3.3.14 — Do you have a policy regarding physical access around non-standard office hours? For example, are permanent members of staff on the premises when third-party suppliers or service providers are working?

In short, section 3.3 focuses on:
- IT governance and outsourced IT oversight,
- security certifications,
- board-level attention to IT and physical security,
- cyber incident response planning,
- past cyber incidents,
- endpoint protection,
- staff training and phishing testing,
- vulnerability and penetration testing,
- unresolved high-risk findings,
- external cyber incident support, and
- physical access controls, including after-hours access.

name: Manager red flags
queries: What 'Red Flag Questions' does the Calamos/Aksia Private Markets Due Diligence Questionnaire tell investors to ask a manager?
description: The Calamos/Aksia Private Markets Due Diligence Questionnaire includes a specific “Red Flag Questions” section telling investors what to ask a manager about personnel turnover, legal/regulatory issues, strategy capacity, fund closure triggers, and the manager’s biggest strategic risk. These questions are meant to surface warning signs that could affect execution, governance, and investor outcomes.
content:
The Calamos/Aksia questionnaire’s “Red Flag Questions” section tells investors to ask a manager these five questions:

1. Have any senior investment professionals left in the last 5 years? If so, please describe.
   - This is aimed at identifying turnover among key investment staff, which can signal instability, cultural issues, succession problems, or weakening execution capability.

2. Are there any history of client complaints, regulatory actions, or pending litigation against your firm or its principals?
   - This is meant to uncover legal, compliance, conduct, or reputational concerns involving the manager or senior leadership.

3. What do you believe the current capacity limit is, and at what asset level would growth impact your ability to continue to deploy the strategy?
   - This tests whether the strategy can absorb more capital without hurting sourcing, underwriting, portfolio construction, or returns.

4. What might cause you to close this fund to new investors?
   - This helps investors understand the manager’s discipline around capacity, market opportunity, and protecting existing investors.

5. What’s the biggest risk to your strategy that keeps you up at night?
   - This seeks the manager’s candid view of the most important vulnerability in the strategy, whether market, liquidity, leverage, valuation, credit, operational, or execution-related.

In short, the questionnaire tells investors to probe five main red-flag areas: key-person departures, complaints/regulatory or legal issues, capacity constraints, reasons for shutting the fund to new money, and the manager’s own assessment of the strategy’s biggest risk.

name: Section 10.0 ESG Questions
queries: What questions are asked under section 10.0 'ESG (Environmental, Social, Governance)' of the NJEDA Life Science Seed Fund due diligence questionnaire (Appendix A)?
description: The relevant evidence shows the ESG section 10.0 questions from the ILPA due diligence questionnaire, which appears to be the basis referenced in the NJEDA Life Science Seed Fund Appendix A due diligence materials. Section 10.0 includes five basic ESG yes/no questions and, in the detailed version, four ESG topic areas with specific sub-questions. Below is a structured list of those questions.
content:
Under section 10.0 “Environmental, Social, & Governance (ESG),” the due diligence questionnaire asks the following questions:

Basic ESG questions (Section 10.0):
1. Does the Firm have an ESG policy (or equivalent CSR/SRI policy)?
2. Is the Firm a signatory to the United Nations Principles for Responsible Investing (UNPRI)?
3. Is the Firm and/or any of its affiliated entities organized in a country that is a member of the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)?
4. Does the Firm have policies that encourage portfolio companies to adopt external standards and codes (such as the United Nations Global Compact)?
5. Does the Firm make formal commitments relating to ESG integration in fund formation contracts, Limited Partnership Agreements, or in side letters when requested by investors?

Detailed ESG questions (Section 10.0, per PRI’s LP Responsible Investment DDQ):

10.1. What are the Firm’s ESG-related policies and how do ESG factors influence its investment beliefs?
- 10.1.1. Does the Firm have a policy that describes its approach to identifying and managing ESG factors within the investment and portfolio management processes? If so, provide a copy. If not, indicate whether the Firm would consider adopting a responsible investment policy.
- 10.1.2. What is the current implementation status of the Firm’s responsible investment policy? Does it have any firm plans to develop its approach towards the management of ESG factors?
- 10.1.3. Does the Firm commit to any international standards, industry (association) guidelines, reporting frameworks, or initiatives that promote responsible investment practices?
- 10.1.4. Does the Firm make formal commitments relating to ESG integration in fund formation contracts, Limited Partnership Agreements, or in side letters when requested by investors?

10.2. How does the Firm identify and manage material ESG-related risk and use ESG factors to create value?
- 10.2.1. How does the Firm define the materiality of ESG factors? Give 2–3 examples of ESG factors that have been identified as material to portfolio companies in the most recent fund.
- 10.2.2. Describe the Firm’s process for identifying and understanding (i) potentially material ESG risks, and (ii) ESG-related opportunities during due diligence.
- 10.2.3. Once identified, how might (i) potentially material ESG risks, and (ii) ESG-related opportunities impact the investment decision?
- 10.2.4. How are ESG risks and/or ESG-related opportunities reported to, considered, and documented by the ultimate decision-making body, such as the Investment Committee?
- 10.2.5. During deal structuring, what is the process for integrating ESG-related considerations into the deal documentation and/or the post-investment action plan?
- 10.2.6. Describe how (i) oversight responsibilities, and (ii) implementation responsibilities for ESG integration are structured within the Firm. List the persons involved and describe their role, position within the organization, and how they are qualified for this role. Describe any external resources the Firm may use.
- 10.2.7. Does the Firm provide training, assistance, and/or external resources to staff to help them understand and identify the relevance and importance of ESG factors in investment activities? If so, describe what level of training is provided.

10.3. How does the Firm contribute to portfolio companies’ management of ESG-related risks and opportunities?
- 10.3.1. Upon investing in a company, would the Firm review existing compliance with sustainability or ethical business guidelines, or introduce new guidelines if necessary?
- 10.3.2. What monitoring processes would the Firm have in place to assess portfolio companies’ management of ESG factors?
- 10.3.3. Give 2–3 examples of how the Firm has contributed to portfolio companies’ management of ESG factors. Specify which initiative(s) the Firm worked with management to identify and instigate; which the Firm supported the portfolio company to achieve (and how); and/or what the portfolio company was already doing that the Firm identified as existing good practice.
- 10.3.4. How does the Firm assess that adequate ESG-related competence exists at the portfolio company level? How does it ensure that portfolio company management devotes sufficient resources to manage ESG factors that have been identified?
- 10.3.5. How does the Firm use its interaction with the board to influence the portfolio company’s management of ESG factors?
- 10.3.6. Does the Firm systematically incorporate ESG considerations into preparations for exit? If yes, describe the approach. If not, explain why.
- 10.3.7. Does the Firm measure whether its approach to ESG factors has affected the financial and/or ESG performance of its investments? If yes, describe how it’s able to determine these outcomes.

10.4. How can LPs monitor and, where necessary, ensure that the Fund is operating consistently with agreed-upon ESG-related policies and practices, including disclosure of ESG-related incidents?
- 10.4.1. Which channels does the Firm use to communicate ESG-related information to LPs? Can the Firm provide samples of ESG-related disclosures from an earlier fund? If not, indicate whether the Firm would consider introducing ESG-related disclosures.

content:
Under the ILPA ESG Assessment Framework, in the “Approach to Policy Review” component:

- At the **Intermediate** level, the GP **conducts a periodic review of its ESG policy every 2–3 years** and **can share recent findings and updates**.
- At the **Advanced** level, the GP **reviews its ESG policy annually** and **can comment on its evolution**, including prior findings, how they were addressed, and how the policy keeps pace with industry developments.

So, the review frequency is:
- **Intermediate:** every **2–3 years**
- **Advanced:** **annually**

name: ILPA DDQ 2.0 ESG topics
queries: What topics does the ILPA DDQ 2.0 cover under its ESG section?
description: The evidence shows that the ILPA DDQ 2.0 includes ESG as its own section and provides the specific topics asked within that section. Those topics focus on ESG policy, integration into investment and portfolio management, risk and opportunity assessment, portfolio company oversight, training/governance, LP reporting, and disclosure of ESG incidents.
content:
The ESG section of the ILPA DDQ 2.0 covers these main topic areas:

- The firm’s ESG-related policies and how ESG factors influence its investment beliefs.
- Whether the firm has a formal responsible investment / ESG policy for identifying and managing ESG factors in investment and portfolio management.
- The current implementation status of that policy and any plans to further develop the firm’s ESG approach.
- Whether the firm commits to international standards, industry guidelines, reporting frameworks, or initiatives that promote responsible investment practices.
- Whether the firm makes formal ESG commitments in fund formation documents, LPAs, or side letters.

It then addresses how the firm identifies and manages material ESG risks and opportunities, including:
- How the firm defines ESG materiality.
- Examples of ESG factors considered material to portfolio companies.
- The process for identifying material ESG risks and ESG-related opportunities during due diligence.
- How identified ESG risks and opportunities affect investment decisions.
- How ESG issues are reported to, considered by, and documented for the ultimate decision-making body, such as the Investment Committee.
- How ESG considerations are integrated into deal documentation and/or post-investment action plans during deal structuring.

The section also covers ESG governance and implementation inside the firm:
- How oversight and implementation responsibilities for ESG integration are structured.
- Who is involved, their roles, seniority, qualifications, and any external resources used.
- Whether staff receive ESG training, assistance, or external support to recognize and evaluate ESG issues in investment activities.

For portfolio companies, the ESG section asks about:
- Whether the firm reviews compliance with sustainability or ethical business guidelines at the time of investment, or introduces new guidelines if needed.
- What monitoring processes are used to assess portfolio companies’ management of ESG factors.
- Examples of how the firm has helped portfolio companies manage ESG factors.
- How the firm assesses whether portfolio companies have sufficient ESG competence and devote enough resources to ESG management.
- How the firm uses board interaction to influence portfolio company ESG management.
- Whether ESG considerations are systematically incorporated into exit preparation.
- Whether the firm measures the effect of its ESG approach on financial and/or ESG performance, and how.

Finally, the section covers LP monitoring and disclosure:
- Which channels the firm uses to communicate ESG-related information to LPs.
- Whether the firm can provide examples of ESG disclosures from prior funds.
- Whether ESG management is included on the LP Advisory Committee and/or Annual General Meeting agenda.
- How the firm discloses and follows up on material ESG incidents to LPs.

In short, the ILPA DDQ 2.0 ESG section covers policy, implementation, diligence, decision-making, portfolio company management, governance, training, performance measurement, LP reporting, and incident disclosure.

name: PRS-STL actuary requirement.
queries: In the Police Retirement System of St. Louis (PRS-STL) actuarial RFP, how many years of experience must the principal actuary have?
description: In the PRS-STL actuarial auditing services RFP, the mandatory minimum qualifications state that the principal actuary assigned to PRS-STL must have at least five years of professional actuarial experience. The same section also requires at least five years of experience testifying before legislative and administrative bodies.
content:
The PRS-STL RFP’s “Mandatory Minimum Qualifications” says the principal actuary assigned to provide services to PRS-STL must have a minimum of five (5) years of professional actuarial experience.

Relevant details from that section:
- The principal actuary must have at least five (5) years of professional actuarial experience.
- The principal actuary must also be:
  - an enrolled actuary,
  - a Member of the American Academy of Actuaries,
  - and an Associate of the Society of Actuaries,
  - with Fellowship in the Society of Actuaries preferred.
- Separately, the RFP also requires the principal actuary to have a minimum of five (5) years of experience testifying before legislative and administrative bodies in support of actuarial positions and/or valuation principles or legislative cost estimates.

So, the direct answer is: five (5) years.

name: Level IV scoring weights.
queries: What are the evaluation criteria and their weights used in Level IV of the LACERS 2025 actuarial consulting services RFP?
description: In Level IV (“Proposed Services and Compensation”) of the LACERS 2025 actuarial consulting services RFP, proposals are evaluated using four criteria with stated weights totaling 100. The evidence directly lists the criteria and their corresponding weights.
content:
For Level IV of the LACERS 2025 actuarial consulting services RFP, titled “Proposed Services and Compensation (“Proposal”),” the evaluation panel scores and ranks firms using these criteria and weights:

- Professionalism — 15
  - Assesses whether the proposer demonstrated professionalism in the RFP response, such as RFP presentation and a well-written summary of the important features of the RFP.

- Proposed Scope of Services Description and Methodology — 30
  - Assesses whether the proposer demonstrated a strong understanding of LACERS’ objectives and provided a proposed methodology and further refinement of the RFP scope of services to meet LACERS’ objectives, project schedules, and budget.

- Qualifications, Experience, and Accomplishments — 35
  - Assesses the strength of the proposer’s experience in providing actuarial services for public pension systems; the demonstrated expertise and knowledge of the proposed team in providing the scope of services and value-add; and the strength of favorable references during the due diligence review process.

- Value of Cost — 20
  - Assesses the relative cost and value shown in the proposed fee. The RFP states this is evaluated on a qualitative basis as well, not only a quantitative basis, and expects the cost proposal to include details of all costs associated with the scope of services.

Total weight: 100.

Context from the RFP:
- Level IV follows earlier review stages: Level I (Administrative Responsiveness), Level II (Review of Qualifications, Experience, and References), and Level III (Interview).
- After Level IV, Level V is final approval by the LACERS Board.
- The RFP notes that interviews may also be conducted as part of Level IV.

- Renewal/extension option: PRS-STL may renew the contract.
- Specific duration of renewal/extension: not stated in the provided text.

A separate document in the evidence set is an OCERS investment consulting RFP, not an actuarial services RFP. It says the initial term would be five years with an option to renew for up to one additional year, but because it concerns investment consulting rather than actuarial services, it should not be treated as directly answering the user’s question about actuarial services RFPs.
